11570:
To opine means to express or state your personal opinion on something — to openly declare what you think or believe about a subject.

It simply means to give your view. When someone opines, they are not reporting a fact. They are sharing what they personally think is true, right, or best. The opinion belongs to them, and they are putting it out into the world.
But There's More to It Than That

If "opine" just meant "to say what you think," we'd have no need for it — we already have words like think, believe, say, and feel. What makes "opine" special is the flavor it adds.

When you say someone opined, you are subtly hinting that they stated their view with a certain confidence and weight — as if they felt their opinion was worth declaring, even if nobody asked for it. There's often a quiet suggestion that the person is being a little self-important, pompous, or overly certain about a view that is, after all, just their personal take.

Think of it this way: thinking something happens inside your head. Saying something is neutral. But opining is a slightly theatrical, self-assured act of putting your view forward, often in formal or elevated language, sometimes with an air of authority.
The Tone: Formal with a Hint of Irony

"Opine" belongs to formal or literary language. You won't hear it much in casual conversation. You'll find it in newspapers, legal writing, formal essays, and books.

And here's the interesting part — writers often use it with a gentle touch of irony or sarcasm. When a journalist writes "the commentator opined that the film was a masterpiece," there's often a subtle, barely-hidden smirk in that sentence. The writer is suggesting that this is merely one person's grand proclamation, not a universal truth.

So the word can be used both seriously and with dry humor, depending on context.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Think / believe — These describe what is happening inside your mind. You can think something privately and tell no one. Opining is always an outward act — you are expressing it.

Say — Completely neutral. You can say anything — a fact, a question, a joke. Opining specifically involves personal viewpoint.

Claim / assert — These suggest you are presenting something as though it were a fact. Opining is softer — it signals clearly that this is personal opinion.

Suggest — This is tentative and gentle. Opining is more confident and declaratory.

So "opine" lives in a specific lane: it is outward, opinion-based, confident, and slightly formal — all at once.

The most common structure is: opine that + [your view]

  • The professor opined that modern architecture had lost its soul.
  • The elderly senator opined that young people no longer respected tradition.
  • She opined that the new policy would do more harm than good.

You can also opine on or about something:

  • He happily opined on everything from food to foreign policy.
  • The critic opined about the novel's weak ending for twenty minutes.

You can also opine without any following clause, simply as a way to describe someone who is in the act of giving their views:

  • "She opined freely whenever given a microphone."

Imagine a retired judge sitting at a dinner party. Nobody asked him, but he leans forward, clears his throat, and declares: "This city's leadership has completely failed its citizens." He says it with full confidence, as if delivering a verdict.

A journalist writing about this dinner would not say he mentioned or whispered that. They would say he opined it — because it was a bold, self-assured expression of personal view, delivered with a certain air of authority. And depending on the journalist's tone, that single word choice could either respect the judge or quietly poke fun at his pompousness.

That is the full life of the word opine — to express a personal opinion, often with confidence, often in formal settings, and often carrying just a faint whiff of someone who is a little too pleased with their own views.
11571:
If someone is opinionated, it means they hold strong opinions about things — and they hold onto them firmly. They don't just have views quietly in their head; they express those views confidently, often without being asked, and they're not easily persuaded to change their mind, even when challenged with solid arguments.

Think of it this way: everyone has opinions. But not everyone is opinionated. What sets an opinionated person apart is a combination of three things working together:

  1. Strong conviction — they don't sit on the fence. They believe their view is clearly right.
  2. Free expression — they voice their views readily, sometimes without waiting for an invitation to do so.
  3. Resistance to change — they hold their position stubbornly, even when others push back.

Remove any one of these, and the person is just "someone with opinions." Put all three together, and you have someone opinionated.
Is It a Positive or Negative Word?

When used to describe a person, "opinionated" almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone. It's not a harsh insult, but it's not really a compliment either. It suggests that the person's confidence tips over into stubbornness, and that they may not genuinely listen to other points of view.

Compare these:

  • "She's confident." → clearly positive
  • "She's opinionated." → slightly critical — implies she's firm to the point of being closed-minded

That said, how negative it sounds depends on the context. In casual conversation, "he's pretty opinionated" might simply mean "he knows what he thinks and isn't shy about it" — said with mild amusement rather than harsh judgment. But the word never fully loses that edge.
Why "Opinionated" Is Different from Just "Having Opinions"

This is the most important distinction to understand.

A person can have strong political beliefs but still genuinely listen to the other side, change their mind when presented with evidence, and engage in calm debate. That person is not really opinionated in the true sense of the word.

An opinionated person, on the other hand, tends to:

  • Share their views without being asked — you didn't invite the topic, but here they are
  • Present their opinion as though it were fact, or as the only sensible position to hold
  • Make the conversation feel one-directional — they're not really curious about your view, they're asserting theirs
  • Be difficult to reason with, because in their mind, the matter is already settled

In short: having opinions is universal; being opinionated is a personality tendency characterized by assertiveness and inflexibility combined.

• "My grandfather is very opinionated about politics — once he's decided something, no argument will change his mind."
  • "She gave such opinionated feedback that it left no room for any other ideas."
  • "He's too opinionated to work well in a team; he never really considers anyone else's suggestions."
  • "I asked her what she thought of the restaurant, but she was so opinionated that it turned into a ten-minute lecture."

In each case, you can feel the slight edge. There's a sense that this person goes beyond simply having views — they impose them, or at least are very reluctant to let them go.

"Opinionated" works well with modifiers:

  • "Slightly opinionated" — has clear, firm views but can still have a real conversation
  • "Very opinionated" — strong views + clear resistance to changing them
  • "Incredibly/outrageously opinionated" — the person essentially steamrolls others in conversation
When Can It Be Used Positively?

Occasionally, "opinionated" is used in a neutral or even admiring way, especially in contexts where decisiveness and strong direction are valued:

  • "We needed an opinionated leader who would make bold calls without endless debate."
  • "She's an opinionated designer — she won't let a project go out the door unless it meets her standards."

Even here, though, there's a subtle undercurrent of "this person is strong-willed and not always easy to deal with." The word very rarely becomes purely flattering. If you want to compliment someone for having conviction, words like decisive, principled, or assertive do a cleaner job.
A Special, Very Common Usage: In Technology

In the world of software and technology, "opinionated" has a specific, widely-used meaning that is neutral or positive.

An opinionated tool, framework, or system is one that has already made strong design decisions for you. It tells you: this is how you will structure things, this is the way things are named, this is the workflow you'll follow. It doesn't leave those choices up to you.

The opposite is called unopinionated (or "flexible") — a tool that gives you freedom to make all those decisions yourself.

Example: "Ruby on Rails is an opinionated web framework — it enforces a specific way of organizing your project."

This is positive in context because an opinionated tool can save enormous time and debate. You don't have to agonize over decisions the tool has already made well.

The connection to the human meaning is clear: just as an opinionated person has already decided what the right way is and won't deviate, an opinionated tool has already decided the "right way" to do things — and it holds firm to it.

Understanding how "opinionated" sits next to related words sharpens the meaning significantly:

Assertive — Being assertive simply means expressing yourself clearly and confidently. It's a positive quality. "Opinionated" goes further, adding the element of stubbornness and the implication that the person isn't truly open to being wrong.

Stubborn — "Stubborn" focuses primarily on the refusal to change, regardless of the topic. "Opinionated" focuses on the having and asserting of strong views. They overlap, but stubbornness is about resistance; being opinionated is about the views themselves combined with resistance.

Outspoken — An outspoken person speaks their mind freely and boldly, but this is often seen as a positive trait — like speaking truth to power, or being honest when others stay silent. "Opinionated" is more about excessive confidence in one's own views, not just willingness to voice them.

Dogmatic — This is a stronger, more formal word. A dogmatic person treats their beliefs as absolutely certain and beyond question — often in the context of ideology, religion, or rigid systems of thought. "Opinionated" is the everyday, lighter version of this.

Headstrong — Headstrong emphasizes acting on your own judgment even when others advise you differently. It's about action as much as views. "Opinionated" is more about expressing and defending views.

Someone opinionated is a person who holds strong, firm views on many things, expresses them freely and assertively, and is resistant to changing them — a trait usually seen as a mild character flaw, suggesting self-assured close-mindedness rather than healthy confidence.
11572: Opium is a powerful, naturally occurring drug extracted from a specific poppy plant. It relieves pain intensely, creates a dreamlike sense of happiness, and is highly addictive. It is the raw source from which many of the world's most significant — and dangerous — drugs are made.

Opium comes from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum), a flowering plant. When the unripe seed pod of this poppy is cut open, it oozes a milky white sap. As that sap dries and oxidizes in the air, it darkens into a sticky, brownish-black paste. That paste is opium.

It is entirely natural — not synthesized in a lab. Inside this paste is a mixture of potent natural chemicals called alkaloids, the most important being morphine and codeine. These are what actually do the work inside the human body.
What it does to the body and mind

The human brain has specific receptor sites — called opioid receptors — which naturally respond to the body's own built-in pain-relieving chemicals. When you take opium, its alkaloids (particularly morphine) bind to these receptors and trigger several powerful effects:

  1. Pain relief — intense and rapid. Even severe, unbearable pain becomes muted or disappears. This is opium's most medically valuable quality.
  2. Euphoria — a profound sense of warmth, happiness, and well-being washes over the user. This is a central reason why opium has been used and abused for millennia.
  3. Deep sedation and calm — the person feels dreamy, relaxed, detached from anxiety and distress.
  4. Slowing of body functions — it suppresses coughs, slows digestion and gut movement, and reduces breathing rate. (This slowing of breathing is what makes an overdose fatal — the person simply stops breathing.)
Why it is so dangerous: addiction

Opium's greatest danger is precisely what makes it seductive: the euphoria it produces is so intense that the brain begins to treat it as a necessity rather than a pleasure.

Here is how addiction develops:

  • With repeated use, the brain gradually stops producing its own natural feel-good chemicals, because opium is doing that job for it. The brain essentially becomes "lazy" about producing these chemicals itself.
  • Now the person needs opium just to feel normal — not even good, just baseline functional.
  • When they stop using it, they experience withdrawal: an agonizing cluster of symptoms including severe muscle cramps, uncontrollable shaking, sweating, nausea, insomnia, and an overwhelming, desperate craving for the drug.
  • The more they use, the more they need (called tolerance) — the same dose stops working, and they need larger amounts to feel the same effect.

This cycle of dependency is what makes opium one of the most addictive substances in human history.
The family of drugs it produces

Opium is essentially a "parent substance." Scientists have used it to isolate, refine, and derive many other drugs. All of these belong to a class called opioids (or narcotics):

  • Morphine — the main alkaloid extracted and purified from opium. It is the gold standard of pain relief in medicine and is used in hospitals worldwide for severe pain, cancer, and end-of-life care.
  • Codeine — a milder alkaloid also found in opium, widely used in cough medicines and weaker painkillers.
  • Heroin — made by chemically processing morphine. It is not found naturally in opium but is derived from it. Far more addictive than morphine and entirely illegal worldwide. It has caused immense human suffering.
  • Synthetic and semi-synthetic opioids — drugs like oxycodone, fentanyl, and methadone are created in laboratories to mimic opium's effects. These are involved in the modern global opioid crisis, in which millions — particularly in the United States — have become addicted to prescription painkillers.

All of these drugs share one thing: they work by acting on the same opioid receptors in the brain that opium acts on.

Despite its dangers, opium and its derivatives have been among the most medically important substances ever discovered. Before modern medicine existed, opium was the world's most effective painkiller — there was simply nothing else like it.

Today, morphine (derived from opium) is on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines — drugs so important that every country should have access to them. It remains irreplaceable for:

  • Post-surgical pain management
  • Cancer pain
  • Severe trauma injuries
  • Palliative (end-of-life comfort) care

The fundamental challenge in medicine is using opium's derivatives precisely enough to relieve suffering without triggering addiction — a balance that is genuinely difficult and often goes wrong.

Opium has shaped civilization in profound ways:

  • Ancient use: Evidence of opium use goes back over 3,500 years to ancient Sumer (modern Iraq), Egypt, and Greece, where it was used both as medicine and in religious rituals.
  • The Opium Wars (1839–1842 and 1856–1860): Britain, which profited enormously from trading opium grown in India into China, fought two wars against China partly to protect and expand this trade. The result was widespread, devastating opium addiction across Chinese society and deep political humiliation for China — events that still shape Chinese national memory today.
  • Opium dens: In the 19th century, public opium-smoking establishments (called "opium dens") existed across Asia, Europe, and America. They were associated with altered states, moral panic, and social decay.
  • Freely available medicine: In the 1800s and early 1900s, opium and its derivatives were sold openly over the counter — in products like laudanum (opium dissolved in alcohol) and even in syrups marketed for teething babies. Addiction was epidemic before laws began restricting it.
  • Afghanistan: Today, Afghanistan produces the vast majority of the world's illicit opium, feeding global heroin markets and funding armed groups.

The word "opium" is also used metaphorically — to describe anything that numbs people's minds, dulls their awareness of reality, or provides passive, intoxicating comfort that discourages critical thought or action.

The most famous example is Karl Marx's phrase: "Religion is the opium of the people" — meaning religion, like opium, soothes pain and provides comfort, but also sedates people into passive acceptance of suffering rather than motivating them to change it.

This metaphor is now used broadly. You might hear things like "social media is the opium of the masses" or "celebrity gossip is the opium of the bored." In each case, the idea is the same: something pleasant and numbing that keeps people distracted and docile.

Opium is a controlled substance — illegal to grow, produce, trade, or possess without special government authorization in virtually every country. It is regulated under international law (the UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961). Limited, government-supervised cultivation is permitted in a few countries specifically to produce pharmaceutical morphine and codeine for medicine.

Illegal cultivation and trafficking of opium is a major global criminal enterprise, connected to organized crime, terrorism financing, and public health crises worldwide.

In one sentence: Opium is a naturally derived, highly addictive drug from the poppy plant that powerfully relieves pain and induces euphoria, and is the source of some of the most medically important and socially devastating substances in human history.

It sits at the intersection of medicine and catastrophe — a substance that has saved countless lives through pain relief and ended, ruined, or diminished countless others through addiction.
11573:
An opponent is a person (or a group) who is against you in a contest, competition, argument, debate, or any situation where two sides are clearly divided.

Think of it this way: whenever there is a structured clash — a game, an election, a debate — the person or team on the other side is your opponent. And importantly, the relationship is mutual: if you are my opponent, then I am also yours.

1. In a contest or competition

This is the most common use. In sports, games, elections, legal proceedings, or debates, your opponent is whoever you are directly competing or contending against.

  • A boxer and the person he is fighting in the ring — they are each other's opponents.
  • Two chess players sitting across a board — each is the other's opponent.
  • Two candidates running for the same political position — each is the other's political opponent.
  • Two teams playing a football match — each team is the other's opponent.

2. Against an idea, policy, or plan

"Opponent" also refers to a person who is publicly against something — not necessarily competing against another person, but opposing a concept, proposal, or course of action.

  • "She is a strong opponent of the death penalty." (She is firmly against it.)
  • "The opponents of the new highway project organized a protest."

In this use, the opponent isn't in a game or a race — they simply stand in opposition to something.

Neutrality. This is perhaps the most important quality of the word. An opponent is not necessarily your enemy. The word describes a structural relationship — you are on opposite sides in a specific context — but it carries no automatic suggestion of hatred, hostility, or ill will. You can deeply respect your opponent. A tennis player may admire the skill of her opponent even while trying to beat her.

A defined context. The opponent relationship exists within a specific situation. Once the game ends, or the debate concludes, the opponent relationship may simply dissolve. Two people who were opponents in a chess tournament can be perfectly friendly strangers afterward.

Directness. An opponent is specifically and directly against you (or your side). This is different from, say, a competitor in a market, who may not even be targeting you personally.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Understanding what makes "opponent" different from nearby words helps you use it precisely.

Opponent vs. Enemy
An enemy implies hatred, hostility, and a desire to cause harm. The word carries emotional weight. An opponent is far more neutral. You face an opponent; you despise an enemy. A rival tennis player is your opponent — calling them your "enemy" would sound extreme and personal.

Opponent vs. Rival
A rival suggests an ongoing, repeated competition — often with a personal or emotional edge, sometimes involving jealousy or ambition. Rivals compete repeatedly over time and are deeply aware of each other. Opponents may face each other just once. Two companies that have competed for decades are rivals; the team you play against this Sunday is your opponent.

Opponent vs. Competitor
A competitor is someone pursuing the same goal or prize as you, but the word doesn't necessarily mean you are directly facing each other. In a race with twenty runners, all nineteen others are your competitors, but the person running directly beside you and matching your pace stride-for-stride might be called your opponent in the heat of the moment. "Competitor" is also very common in business contexts (other companies selling similar products), while "opponent" feels more natural in structured contests.

Opponent vs. Adversary
An adversary is more formal and serious. It suggests a sustained, significant opposition — often in high-stakes situations like politics, law, or war. All adversaries could loosely be called opponents, but not all opponents are adversaries. You wouldn't normally call your chess partner your "adversary."

• "Before the match, the coach told us to study our opponent's weaknesses."
  • "My debate opponent made several strong points, and I had to think quickly to respond."
  • "The senator's opponents voted against every bill she introduced."
  • "He treated his opponent with respect, shaking hands both before and after the game."
  • "She is a well-known opponent of online censorship and has written books on the subject."
  • "Our opponents in the final round are the defending champions — this will not be easy."
  • "The lawyer prepared carefully, knowing her opponent in court was highly experienced."
Common Collocations (Words That Often Appear with "Opponent")

These are word combinations you will encounter frequently:

  • Formidable opponent — a very strong, difficult-to-beat opponent
  • Worthy opponent — an opponent who deserves respect because of their skill or strength
  • Political opponent — someone opposing you in the political arena
  • Face your opponent — to confront or go up against them
  • Defeat/beat your opponent — to win against them
  • Underestimate your opponent — to think your opponent is weaker than they actually are (usually a mistake)

When referring to more than one, you simply say opponents.

  • "Our opponents played brilliantly tonight."
  • "She has always treated her opponents fairly."

An opponent is anyone who is on the opposing side from you in a contest, game, election, debate, or structured conflict — or anyone who formally stands against an idea or policy you support. The word is neutral in tone: it describes a position (opposite to yours) without implying hatred. It is tied to a specific context and often temporary. It sits in a family of similar words — rival, enemy, adversary, competitor — but is the most balanced and broadly usable among them.
11574:
"Opportune" describes something that happens or is done at exactly the right time — a time that is perfectly suited to a purpose, a need, or a situation. When something is opportune, the timing is so well-matched to the circumstances that it makes things easier, more effective, or more likely to succeed.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it is fundamentally about timing. Something isn't opportune just because it's good — it's opportune because it's good at this particular moment, and that moment makes all the difference.
Breaking it down with a simple image

Imagine you've been trying to ask your boss for a raise, but you've been waiting for the right moment. One day, your boss walks in extremely happy because the company just landed a huge contract. You think: "Now is the time." That moment — right then, when your boss is in high spirits and the company is doing well — is an opportune moment. The timing lines up perfectly with your goal. If you had asked the week before, when the company was struggling, the timing would have been wrong. But now, it's just right.

That feeling of "just right timing" is the heart of opportune.
What can be described as opportune?

The word is most naturally attached to time-related nouns. You will most often hear or read:

"An opportune moment" — the most common pairing. It refers to a specific point in time that is ideal for doing something.

"An opportune time" — slightly broader than a moment, but same idea. A period or point when conditions are favorable.

"An opportune occasion" — a particular event or situation that happens to be well-suited to doing something.

You can also describe an arrival, a discovery, a silence, or an interruption as opportune if the timing of that thing is what makes it valuable. For example, a rainstorm can be opportune for a farmer whose fields are dry. A phone call can be opportune if it comes exactly when you needed advice. The common thread is always: the timing fits the need.
The key nuance — it's not just "good," it's "good right now"

This is the sharpest edge of the word, and it's worth pausing on. "Opportune" is not a synonym for simply "good," "helpful," or "useful." A warm coat is useful, but you wouldn't call it opportune unless it appeared at the exact moment you were freezing. Opportune always implies that the timing of something is what gives it its value.

Think of it this way: the same action, the same event, or the same word can be opportune in one moment and completely useless — or even harmful — in another. Offering someone a joke might be opportune when they're stressed and need lightening up, but deeply inopportune at a funeral. The word is asking you to pay attention to when, not just what.

The opposite of opportune is inopportune, which means happening at a bad or wrong time. An inopportune moment is one where the timing works against you. If your phone rings loudly during a job interview, that is an inopportune interruption. If you bring up a sensitive topic right when someone is already upset, that is an inopportune time to do so. Understanding this opposite locks in the meaning of opportune even more firmly: it lives entirely in the world of timing.

Opportune is a positive word. It suggests that the timing is genuinely good — not just acceptable, but notably well-suited to the situation. When you call a moment "opportune," you're saying that if you had to design circumstances to make this action or event most effective, you'd have chosen this moment. It carries a sense of fortune or luck aligning with purpose.

You can intensify it — "a most opportune moment," "a perfectly opportune time" — to emphasize just how ideal the timing is. But even on its own, the word already leans strongly positive.
How opportune differs from similar words

Several words are close to opportune but not identical.

Timely is the nearest relative. Something timely arrives or happens before it's too late — it beats a deadline or prevents a problem. Opportune is slightly richer: it doesn't just mean "not too late," it means the timing is actively, specifically favorable. A timely warning stops danger; an opportune warning does so at the ideal moment when it can do the most good.

Well-timed is nearly identical to opportune and can often be swapped for it. Opportune is simply the more formal and literary of the two.

Convenient means easy or suitable for someone's needs, but it lacks the sense of a specific moment aligning with circumstances. Convenient is about ease; opportune is about timing.

Favorable describes conditions being good, but doesn't pin it to a specific moment in time the way opportune does.

None of these words are wrong to know alongside opportune, but the thing that makes opportune itself is always that precise, well-matched, well-timed quality.
One important word to not confuse it with

Do not confuse opportune with opportunistic. They share a root, but they are very different in meaning and tone.

Opportune is neutral-to-positive and simply means well-timed. Opportunistic, on the other hand, describes a person or behavior that selfishly takes advantage of a situation — often in a calculating or unprincipled way. Calling someone "opportunistic" is usually a criticism. Calling a moment "opportune" is simply a description of good timing. They are not interchangeable.

Opportune is a moderately formal word. You'll encounter it in books, articles, speeches, and careful writing. In very casual conversation, people are more likely to say "good timing" or "the right moment," but opportune fits naturally in professional, academic, and literary contexts. It never sounds out of place in writing.
Putting it all together — examples in context

"She arrived at an opportune moment — the meeting had just started and nothing important had been said yet."
Here, her timing was ideal because she didn't miss anything.

"He waited patiently for an opportune time to raise the issue with his manager."
He was looking for a moment when conditions — the manager's mood, the workload, the atmosphere — would make his request most likely to succeed.

"The discovery of water was opportune for the hikers, who had nearly run out of supplies."
The discovery happened exactly when it was most needed, which is what makes it opportune rather than just fortunate.

"This is not the most opportune moment to bring that up."
A gentle way of saying the timing is wrong — the circumstances right now are not well-suited to whatever is being suggested.

In summary: something is opportune when its timing is just right — when the moment aligns so well with a need, a goal, or a situation that things are made easier, more effective, or more successful as a direct result. The word lives entirely in the realm of timing, and its quiet power comes from how precisely it captures that feeling of "this is exactly the right moment."
11575:
Opportunism is the habit or practice of spotting a favorable situation and grabbing it for personal gain — but doing so without caring much about whether it's fair, ethical, or consistent with your own stated beliefs and values.

The key word hiding inside it is opportunity — a chance, an opening, a moment where something useful can be gotten. An opportunist is someone who is always scanning for these openings and pouncing on them the moment they appear, regardless of the cost to others or to their own integrity.
What Makes It "Opportunism" and Not Just "Being Smart"

This is the most important distinction to understand, and most learners miss it.

Taking advantage of a good opportunity is something everyone does, and it's perfectly fine. You see a sale on something you need — you buy it. That's just being sensible.

Opportunism is different. It crosses a line. The crossing happens in one or more of these ways:

1. Principles are abandoned for personal gain.
An opportunist doesn't have a fixed moral compass. They shift their position, loyalty, or behavior based on whatever benefits them right now, not based on what they actually believe is right. Today they stand for one thing; tomorrow, when the wind changes, they stand for the opposite — because the opposite now serves them better.

2. Others are exploited, often unfairly.
Opportunism frequently involves taking advantage of someone else's weakness, desperation, or misfortune. You don't just grab a chance — you grab a chance at someone else's expense, often when they are least able to defend themselves.

3. The ends justify the means, always.
The opportunist's reasoning is simple: "If I can benefit from this, I will." There is little or no pause to ask: "Should I?" or "Is this right?" or "What does this make me?"
The Tone: Is It a Bad Word?

Almost always, yes. Opportunism carries a strong negative connotation in most contexts. When someone calls a politician, a business, or a person an "opportunist," it is rarely a compliment. It implies that the person is:

  • Unprincipled (they have no real values, only interests)
  • Self-serving (their own gain comes first, always)
  • Unreliable (you can't trust them, because their loyalty is for sale)
  • Potentially exploitative (they will use people when it suits them)

However, there are a small number of contexts where the word is used more neutrally — for example, in biology ("opportunistic infections" are infections that strike when the body's defenses are weak — no moral judgment there), or sometimes in military strategy ("opportunistic attack" simply means striking when a gap in the enemy's defense appears). But in everyday human and social contexts — politics, relationships, business — it is almost always a criticism.

In Politics:
A politician promises to protect environmental laws to win votes from environmentalists. The moment they are elected and a powerful oil company offers them money and influence, they quietly vote to weaken those same laws. They didn't actually believe in the environmental cause — they just used it when it was useful. That is political opportunism.

In Business:
A city is hit by a hurricane. A supplier immediately doubles the price of bottled water and generators, knowing people are desperate and have no choice but to pay. They are not solving a problem out of goodwill — they are exploiting a crisis for profit. This is often called crisis opportunism or predatory opportunism.

In Personal Relationships:
Your friend goes through a difficult breakup and is emotionally vulnerable. Someone who has always wanted to date them suddenly appears, showering them with attention — not because they genuinely care, but because they recognize this as the perfect moment to get what they want from someone whose defenses are down. That is personal opportunism.

In Workplaces:
A colleague takes full credit for a team project the moment the manager praises it, even though the whole team contributed equally. They saw an opening to advance their reputation and grabbed it without hesitation or fairness. Opportunism.
The Spectrum: From Mild to Deeply Troubling

Opportunism exists on a spectrum.

On the milder end, it might just mean someone is a little too quick to promote themselves or bend their opinions to match whoever is in power. Annoying, slightly dishonest, but not catastrophic.

On the severe end, it describes people who systematically exploit others' suffering, betray trust for personal advancement, or change their moral positions completely based on what's profitable. Historical examples include political leaders who supported whichever side was winning a war, regardless of which side stood for justice.

The severity of opportunism depends on:

  • How much harm it causes others
  • How deeply it betrays trust or stated values
  • Whether the person is exploiting genuine vulnerability

Since you want full mastery:

  • Opportunism (noun) — the practice or habit itself. "His rise to power was built on pure opportunism."
  • Opportunist (noun) — the person who practices it. "She's a brilliant opportunist — she always knows which way the wind is blowing."
  • Opportunistic (adjective) — describing the nature of an action or person. "It was an opportunistic attack, launched the moment the guard was down."
  • Opportunistically (adverb) — describing how something is done. "He opportunistically switched parties right before the election."
A Final Way to Lock It In

Think of opportunism this way: imagine someone who has no fixed address. They don't live in any one place — they sleep wherever the warmest bed is that night. An opportunist is morally similar. They have no fixed principles. They stand wherever it is most advantageous to stand at any given moment. They are always moving toward the next benefit, and away from any cost.

The word captures something specific and slightly unsettling about human nature — the tendency, in some people more than others, to treat every situation primarily as a resource to be mined for personal advantage, with conscience coming in a distant second.
11576:
An opportunist is a person who spots a situation that could benefit them and quickly acts on it — usually without worrying too much about whether it is fair, ethical, or consistent with what they previously believed or promised.

Think of it this way: most people wait for the "right" moment based on their values or principles. An opportunist, on the other hand, lets the moment itself decide what they do. They ask, "What can I get out of this?" rather than "Is this the right thing to do?"

The key idea hiding inside this word is self-interest over principle.

An opportunist is not just someone who "takes a chance" or "grabs a good deal." That alone would make someone simply smart or resourceful. What truly defines an opportunist is this combination:

  • They act primarily for personal gain.
  • They are flexible with their values — meaning they will switch positions, change loyalties, or ignore ethics if it helps them.
  • They move fast when they see an advantage, without much hesitation or moral reflection.
  • They often take advantage of other people's weaknesses, misfortune, or lack of awareness.

So the word carries a mostly negative tone. When you call someone an opportunist, you are usually criticising them — suggesting they are self-serving, calculating, and not entirely trustworthy.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

The word is used across many areas of life. Here are clear examples:

In politics: A politician who has always publicly supported free healthcare suddenly switches their position when a powerful and wealthy opposition party offers them a senior role. They didn't change their mind because of new evidence — they changed it because it was useful to do so. That's opportunism.

In business: A company sees that a competitor has just collapsed due to a scandal. Instead of pausing respectfully, they immediately swoop in, poach that company's best employees, and run advertisements directly targeting the rival's confused customers. They turned someone else's disaster into their own profit. That's opportunistic behaviour.

In friendships/relationships: Imagine someone who only shows up in your life when they need something from you — a favour, money, a connection — but disappears when you need help. They are treating your friendship as a resource to exploit whenever convenient. People often call such a person an opportunist.

In sports: A footballer who has been playing for a national team for years suddenly switches to represent a different country the moment that country qualifies for the World Cup and the player's original country doesn't. The switch is not about love for the new country — it's about seizing a chance to compete on the biggest stage. Sports commentators would likely call this opportunistic.
The Tone: Negative, but Not Always Equally So

The word sits on a spectrum of negativity, not all at the same level.

At the milder end, someone might be called an opportunist simply because they act fast and put themselves first — a little selfish, but not deeply harmful. In some business contexts, people even use the word with a hint of grudging respect: "She's a sharp opportunist — she saw the market gap before anyone else." Here the criticism is softened.

At the more serious end, an opportunist can be someone who exploits the vulnerable, betrays trust, or causes real harm to others — all in pursuit of personal gain. Here the word is a strong moral criticism.

The common thread at every level: personal advantage comes before loyalty, fairness, or principle.
How It Differs from Simply Being Ambitious or Resourceful

This is an important distinction.

An ambitious person works hard, plans ahead, and pursues their goals — but typically within a consistent set of values. They build something.

A resourceful person finds creative solutions with what's available. They are clever and adaptable — but not at the expense of others.

An opportunist, however, is defined by how they pursue their goals: by watching for gaps, weaknesses, or lucky moments in the world around them and exploiting them — often at the cost of others, or at the cost of their own stated principles.

The difference is not just what they want, but how they are willing to get it.

Since you're learning, it helps to know the word's family:

  • Opportunist (noun) → the person: "He is a shameless opportunist."
  • Opportunistic (adjective) → describing the behaviour or the person: "That was an opportunistic move." / "She is highly opportunistic."
  • Opportunism (noun) → the practice or habit itself: "His political career was built on opportunism rather than conviction."

If you're ever unsure whether someone qualifies as an opportunist, ask this:

"Is this person doing this because it aligns with their values — or simply because the moment makes it advantageous for them?"

If the answer is the latter, especially if someone else is being used or hurt in the process, you are almost certainly looking at opportunist behaviour.

An opportunist is someone who prioritises personal gain above principles, seizes advantages as they appear — especially from situations of weakness, crisis, or change in others — and is willing to be flexible with their ethics or loyalties to get ahead. The word is most commonly used as a criticism, suggesting that the person is clever but not trustworthy, self-serving but not principled.
11577:
Opportunistic describes someone (or something) that takes advantage of a situation as soon as it arises — not because of careful planning or strong principles, but simply because the chance is there.

Think of it this way: an opportunistic person doesn't create situations. They exploit them the moment they appear, often acting quickly and flexibly, but usually without much concern for fairness, loyalty, or ethics.
The Connotation — Is It a Bad Word?

This depends entirely on the context.

When used to describe human behavior, it almost always carries a negative or suspicious tone. Calling a person opportunistic is rarely a compliment. It implies they are self-serving — that they will bend their values, switch sides, or take advantage of others the moment it benefits them. It suggests a lack of principle.

However, when used in science (biology or medicine), it is completely neutral — just a factual description of a pattern.

This is the most common everyday use.

An opportunistic person watches for openings and exploits them for personal gain, regardless of whether it is the right thing to do, or whether it hurts others. They don't necessarily plan to do wrong — they simply don't let ethics, loyalty, or fairness stop them when an opportunity appears.

Examples:

  • A colleague who takes credit for your idea the moment you present it in a meeting — not because they had a scheme, but because the opening was there — is being opportunistic.
  • A politician who suddenly changes their stated beliefs to match whatever opinion is popular at the time, purely to gain more votes, is acting opportunistically.
  • A friend who is warm and helpful to you only when they need something from you, and distant otherwise, is an opportunistic friend.

The thread connecting all of these is: personal advantage comes first, principles come second (or not at all).
The Key Distinction: Opportunistic vs. Simply Ambitious

This is an important line to draw.

An ambitious person sets goals, works hard, and grabs opportunities — but usually with some code of conduct. They want to succeed, but they care how they succeed.

An opportunistic person, on the other hand, is more reactive and unprincipled. They don't necessarily work toward a goal — they simply pounce the moment a chance appears, with little regard for whether their action is fair, honest, or consistent with what they claimed to believe.

In short: ambition is about drive. Opportunism is about exploitation.

When describing crimes, the word is used in a more neutral, descriptive way — meaning the crime was unplanned.

An opportunistic crime is one where the criminal didn't set out to commit a crime that day. They simply spotted an easy opening and acted on it. For example, someone who notices an unlocked car with a wallet sitting on the seat and steals it — without having planned to steal anything — has committed an opportunistic theft. The situation created the crime, not prior scheming.

This is why it's used in a more neutral tone here — it describes the nature of the act (unplanned, situational), not necessarily a character flaw.

In nature, an opportunistic species or opportunistic feeder is one that is highly adaptable — it doesn't rely on one specific food source or habitat. It eats or lives wherever and whenever resources become available.

A crow is a great example. It doesn't specialize. It eats scraps, insects, grains, carrion — whatever is accessible. It thrives because it is flexible and exploits whatever the environment offers at any given moment.

Here, "opportunistic" is a compliment of sorts — it means resilient and adaptable.

This is a very specific and important use of the word.

An opportunistic infection is one caused by a germ (bacteria, virus, or fungus) that does not normally cause illness in a healthy person — but causes serious disease when the body's immune system is weakened.

These germs are called opportunistic because they "seize the opportunity" created by the body's vulnerability. They cannot overpower a strong immune system, so they wait, essentially, until the defenses are down — then they strike.

This is why patients with HIV/AIDS, or those undergoing chemotherapy (both of which weaken immunity), are especially at risk for opportunistic infections. The same germs that would be harmless to a healthy person become life-threatening to them.
How to Use It in Sentences

• "He was an opportunistic investor — he never had a strategy, he just bought whatever seemed cheap that day."
  • "The robbery was opportunistic — the thief saw an open window and climbed in on impulse."
  • "Her critics accused her of being opportunistic, saying she only supported the cause when it was politically convenient."
  • "Crows are opportunistic feeders that can survive in almost any environment."
  • "The patient developed an opportunistic infection after weeks of chemotherapy."
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Opportunistic = taking advantage of a situation the moment it appears, driven by self-interest or circumstance rather than planning or principle — a negative quality in people, a neutral or positive trait in nature and science.
11578:
To oppose something means to be actively against it — not just in your mind, but through your words, stance, or actions. When you oppose something, you push back against it, resist it, or try to challenge or stop it.

Here's an important distinction: if you simply dislike something quietly and do nothing about it, that's not quite opposing. To oppose is to take a side — the side that is against something — and to clearly express or act on that position.
The Key Idea: Two Sides in Tension

Whenever "oppose" appears, there are always two sides facing each other. You, and the thing or person you are against. This tension — this push and pull — is the soul of the word. The two sides could be people, ideas, groups, or forces working against each other.
How "Oppose" Is Used in Different Situations

1. Opposing an idea, plan, or decision — this is the most common use. It means you disagree with something and actively work against it.

  • Many citizens opposed the new tax law.
  • The scientists opposed the flawed theory.
  • She opposed every change the committee proposed.

2. Opposing a person — standing against someone directly, especially in a competition, election, or conflict.

  • He will oppose the current mayor in the upcoming election.
  • The underdog was chosen to oppose the reigning champion.

3. Opposing in a debate or argument — arguing against what someone says.

  • The lawyer opposed every claim made by the other side.

4. Physical opposition — blocking or resisting something by force or position.

  • The soldiers opposed the enemy's advance into the city.
  • A locked door opposed his entry.
How Strongly Can You Oppose Something?

The word "oppose" on its own doesn't tell you how intensely someone is against something — that comes from the words used around it. Pay attention to these:

  • slightly opposed → mild disagreement
  • strongly opposed / firmly opposed → serious, clear resistance
  • bitterly opposed / vehemently opposed → deep, intense resistance, often with emotion

So "she opposed the plan" and "she bitterly opposed the plan" both use the same verb, but the second one tells you she felt very strongly about it.
The Very Common Phrase: "As Opposed To"

This phrase deserves special attention because it is used constantly in everyday English, and its meaning is slightly different from the main verb.

"As opposed to" means "in contrast to" or "rather than." It highlights a clear difference or preference between two things. Importantly, there is no conflict here — it simply draws a distinction.

  • I prefer working in the morning, as opposed to the evening.
  • This is a health issue, as opposed to a lifestyle choice.
  • She wanted a small wedding, as opposed to a large celebration.

Think of it as a way of saying: "Let's be clear — I'm talking about THIS one, not THAT one."

Learning a word fully means knowing its relatives. Here is the family of "oppose":

Opponent (noun) — a person who opposes you; your rival or adversary in a competition, debate, or conflict.
He was a skilled opponent who never gave up easily.

Opposition (noun) — this has two uses. First, it means the act of opposing something. Second, it refers to the group of people who are against something, especially in politics.
The proposal faced fierce opposition from the public.
The opposition party voted against the bill.

Opposed (adjective) — used to describe someone who is against something, or two things that are against each other.
I am completely opposed to the idea.
The two sides held opposed views on the matter.

Opposing (adjective / present participle) — describes something or someone that is on the other side.
The opposing team played brilliantly.
They came from opposing backgrounds but became close friends.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Think of the prefix "op-" as meaning "against" and the image it creates: two things facing each other from opposite sides. Whenever you see or use "oppose," picture two forces or two people standing face to face, each pushing against the other. That image captures the word perfectly.
11579:
Opposition means being against something or someone — a force, action, or position that pushes back, resists, or stands on the opposite side.

Think of it like a tug-of-war. One side pulls one way; the other side pulls the other way. The tension between those two sides — that is opposition.

1. Resistance or disagreement toward something

This is the most common use. When people object to an idea, a plan, a decision, or an action, their pushback is called opposition.

  • "There was strong opposition to the new traffic law."
  • "The factory faced opposition from local residents who were worried about pollution."
  • "Despite all the opposition, she went ahead with her decision."

Here, opposition means the act of being against something. It doesn't have to be a physical fight — it can be verbal disagreement, protest, a vote against, or simply an attitude of refusal.

2. A person or group that opposes you

Opposition can also refer to the people who are against you — your opponents, your rivals, the other side.

  • "The team studied the opposition carefully before the final match."
  • "He faced no real opposition in the race — everyone agreed with him."

Here, "the opposition" is a collective noun — it means the opposing side as a whole.

3. In politics — the official opposing party

In countries that follow a parliamentary system (like India, the UK, or Australia), "the Opposition" (often written with a capital O) has a very specific meaning: the main political party or group that is not in power, but sits in the legislature and challenges the ruling government.

  • "The Opposition demanded an explanation from the Prime Minister."
  • "She is the leader of the Opposition."
  • "The bill was passed despite strong opposition from the opposition benches."

This is a formal, institutionalized role. The Opposition is not just informally against the government — they are officially designated as the counterbalancing force in a democracy. Their job is to question, scrutinize, and challenge the party in power.

4. A state of contrast or being on opposite sides

Opposition can also describe a condition where two things are placed against each other — where they are fundamentally contrary to one another. This is a slightly more abstract use.

  • "The two philosophies stand in direct opposition to each other."
  • "His quiet lifestyle was in opposition to his loud, chaotic personality at work."

This use doesn't necessarily imply conflict — it can simply mean that two things are opposite in nature, like light and darkness, silence and noise, or order and chaos.

5. In astronomy — a specific planetary position

In astronomy, opposition has a precise technical meaning: it is the moment when a planet (like Mars or Jupiter) is positioned directly opposite the Sun, with Earth in the middle. At this point, the planet is closest to Earth and appears largest and brightest in the night sky.

  • "Mars will be at opposition next month — the best time to observe it through a telescope."

You won't use this meaning in everyday speech, but it's worth knowing if you ever read about space.
The Deeper Texture of the Word

Understanding opposition fully means understanding what it implies:

It requires two sides. There can be no opposition in isolation. Something can only be in opposition to something else. It's a relational word — it describes a relationship between two forces, ideas, people, or groups.

Opposition does not always mean hatred or violence. It can range from a mild difference of opinion all the way to fierce, sustained conflict. A person can be in opposition to a policy while still being respectful. A political opposition party debates in a parliament, not on a battlefield.

Opposition implies seriousness. If someone has "a little disagreement," you wouldn't call it opposition. The word carries weight — it suggests that the resistance is real, meaningful, and has some force or commitment behind it.

Opposition can be organized or unorganized. An individual can personally be in opposition to something. But opposition can also be a collective, structured force — like a political party, a union, a protest movement, or a rival team.

• "In opposition to" — means against, or in contrast to.
    "She voted in opposition to the proposed change."
  • "Face opposition" — to encounter resistance.
    "The new policy faced immediate opposition."
  • "Strong/fierce/stiff opposition" — opposition that is intense and hard to overcome.
    "The bill met stiff opposition in parliament."
  • "Meet with opposition" — to encounter pushback when you try to do something.
    "His proposal met with opposition from all sides."
  • "The leader of the opposition" — the head of the main opposing political party.

If you ever see "opposition" in a sentence and want to know which meaning is intended, ask yourself:

  • Is it talking about an action or attitude of being against something? → It means resistance or disagreement.
  • Is it referring to people who are against you? → It means the opposing side/group.
  • Is it in a political context, especially with a capital O? → It means the official opposing party.
  • Is it describing two things that are contrary in nature? → It means a state of contrast.
  • Is it in an astronomy article about planets? → It means a specific alignment in space.

Opposition is fundamentally about being on the other side — whether that means resisting an idea, being the rival team, holding the role of the political party that challenges those in power, or simply being the contrasting force to something else. It is a word about conflict, contrast, and counterforce — always involving two sides, and always implying that one is pushing back against the other.
